entry.gloss: how high or low a sound is
entry.def: How high or low a sound is, which depends on how fast it vibrates: faster vibrations sound higher. On the staff, higher pitches are written higher.
A way of naming each octave with a number that changes at every C: middle C is C4, the B just below it is B3, and the A above it, to which orchestras tune, is A4.

entry.gloss: sign before a note that raises or lowers it
entry.def: A sharp, flat, natural, double sharp or double flat written before a note. It applies to every later note on the same line or space until the end of the bar.

figure.caption: The sharp still applies to the third note; the natural cancels it, and the barline ends it.

entry.gloss: raises a note by a half step
entry.def: The sign ♯, which raises a note by a half step: F# is a half step above F, the black key just to its right on the piano.

entry.gloss: lowers a note by a half step
entry.def: The sign ♭, which lowers a note by a half step: Bb is a half step below B, the black key just to its left on the piano.
The sign ♮, which cancels an earlier sharp or flat, from an accidental or from the key signature, so that the note is played unaltered.

figure.caption: The natural cancels the sharp of the key signature.

entry.gloss: raises a note by two half steps
entry.def: The sign 𝄪, which raises a note by two half steps, a whole step: F## sounds the same as G. It is typically needed when a note that already has a sharp in the key is raised again.

entry.gloss: lowers a note by two half steps
entry.def: The sign 𝄫, which lowers a note by two half steps, a whole step: Bbb sounds the same as A.

entry.gloss: the smallest step: between adjacent piano keys
entry.def: The smallest interval in common-practice music: the distance between two adjacent keys on the piano, such as E–F or C–C#. Called a semitone in British English.
An interval of two half steps, such as C–D or E–F#. Called a whole tone, or simply a tone, in British English.

entry.gloss: half step between notes of the same letter
entry.def: A half step between two notes with the same letter name, such as C–C# or B–Bb. As an interval it is an augmented unison. Called a chromatic semitone in British English.
A half step between two notes with neighboring letter names, such as E–F or C–Db: a minor second. Called a diatonic semitone in British English.
Notes are enharmonic, or enharmonic equivalents, when they sound the same but are written differently, such as F# and Gb or E# and F. Intervals, chords and keys can be enharmonic too.

entry.gloss: using notes from outside the key
entry.def: Using notes that do not belong to the key, made by adding accidentals; the opposite of diatonic. A melody that moves by half steps is also called chromatic.
